Who’s Who in the New Testament

A companion to the New Testament studies · dates are approximate and scholars vary

How to use this book

This book gathers 87 of the people who matter most to the gospel story and its spread, along with the rulers, Romans and officials who shaped the world they lived in. It is arranged in ten parts. Each entry gives the person’s role, dates, places and the books where they appear, a short account of who they were, one key verse from the American Standard Version and passages to read.

The lined column beside each page is for your notes. The time maps and maps show how everyone fits together, and the contents at the front lists every name, including other names a person goes by.

Who’s inside

PartPeople
Part 1Jesus and His Family: Jesus of Nazareth, Mary, mother of Jesus, Joseph, John the Baptist, Zechariah and Elizabeth
Part 2The Twelve Apostles: Simon Peter, Andrew, James, son of Zebedee, John, son of Zebedee, Philip the apostle, Bartholomew (Nathanael), Matthew (Levi), Thomas, James, son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus (Judas, son of James), Simon the Zealot, Judas Iscariot, Matthias
Part 3Women Who Followed and Served: Mary Magdalene, Mary, Martha and Lazarus, Joanna and Susanna, Mary, mother of John Mark, Tabitha (Dorcas), Lydia, Phoebe, Lois and Eunice
Part 4The Jerusalem Church and the First Spread: James, the brother of Jesus, Jude, Stephen, Philip the evangelist, The Ethiopian official, Ananias of Damascus, Agabus
Part 5Paul and His Coworkers: Paul (Saul of Tarsus), Barnabas, Silas (Silvanus), Timothy, Titus, Luke, John Mark, Priscilla and Aquila, Apollos, Tychicus, Epaphras, Epaphroditus, Aristarchus, Philemon and Onesimus, Erastus, Demas
Part 6Jewish Leaders: Annas, Caiaphas, Gamaliel, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Ananias, son of Nedebaeus
Part 7The Herod Family: Herod the Great, Archelaus, Herod Antipas, Herodias and her daughter, Philip the tetrarch, Herod Agrippa I, Herod Agrippa II and Bernice
Part 8The Roman Emperors: Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula (Gaius), Claudius, Nero, Vespasian, Titus, Domitian
Part 9Roman Governors, Soldiers and Officials: Quirinius, Pontius Pilate, The centurions of the Gospels, Cornelius, Sergius Paulus, Gallio, The town clerk and the Asiarchs of Ephesus, Claudius Lysias, Felix, Festus, Julius the centurion, Publius
Part 10Opponents and Others Along the Way: Simon the sorcerer, Elymas (Bar-Jesus), Demetrius the silversmith, Alexander the coppersmith, Diotrephes

The time map: the rulers

Red bars are rulers named in the New Testament; grey bars are rulers in the background. From AD 41 to 44 Agrippa I ruled Judea as king, so there was no Roman governor. From AD 6 Rome appointed and removed the high priests; from AD 41 the Herodian kings did so.

The time map: the gospel’s people

The church spread through the same decades as the reigns on the previous chart: Pentecost under Tiberius, Paul's journeys under Claudius and Nero, Revelation under Domitian.

Map: the Holy Land

Jesus’ family, the Twelve, the Herods and the governors of Judea, placed where they lived and worked.

Map: the Roman world

How far the gospel traveled in one generation, and where Paul’s coworkers, the emperors and Roman officials appear.

Groups and titles you’ll meet

NameWho they were
PhariseesA lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and the oral traditions. Popular with ordinary people; believed in resurrection and angels. Paul had been one.
SadduceesThe priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple. Accepted only the written law and denied the resurrection. Cooperated closely with Rome.
ScribesExperts in the law who copied, taught and interpreted it; most were Pharisees. Also called lawyers or teachers of the law.
SanhedrinThe ruling council in Jerusalem, about seventy members, led by the high priest. Tried Jesus, Peter and John, Stephen and Paul.
HerodiansSupporters of the Herod family's rule. Joined Pharisees in trying to trap Jesus over paying taxes to Caesar.
ZealotsJews who were zealous for the law and later fought Rome openly in the revolt of AD 66–70.
Tax collectorsLocal men who bought the right to collect tolls and customs and often overcharged. Seen as traitors and sinners.
SamaritansDescendants of northern Israelites who worshiped at Mount Gerizim and accepted only the books of Moses. Long hostile to Jews.
God-fearersGentiles who worshiped Israel's God and attended synagogue without becoming full converts, like Cornelius and Lydia. Many were early believers.
CaesarThe title of the Roman emperor, taken from Julius Caesar's family name.
Prefect, procuratorThe Roman governor of a smaller province such as Judea. Pilate was a prefect; Felix and Festus were procurators.
ProconsulThe governor of a senatorial province such as Cyprus, Achaia or Asia. Luke uses this title correctly for Sergius Paulus and Gallio.
Tetrarch, ethnarchTitles for lesser rulers under Rome. Herod's sons Antipas and Philip were tetrarchs; Archelaus was ethnarch.
Centurion, tribuneA centurion commanded about eighty soldiers; a tribune commanded a cohort of about a thousand.
AsiarchsWealthy leading men of the province of Asia who oversaw festivals and the emperor cult.

parts.title: Jesus and His Family
parts.intro: The gospel begins with a family in a small Galilean town and a relative preaching in the wilderness. Jesus' brothers James and Jude, who became leaders after the resurrection, appear with the Jerusalem church in Part 4.

people.name: Jesus of Nazareth
people.role: The Messiah, the center of the gospel
facts: Born about 6–4 BC · ministry about AD 27–30 · crucified about AD 30 (others date the ministry AD 29–33)
Every book of the New Testament (3 John refers to him only as “the Name”)
paras: Born in Bethlehem during the last years of Herod the Great and raised in Nazareth as the son of a carpenter. After his baptism by John he preached the kingdom of God across Galilee and Judea, healed the sick, taught in parables and called twelve disciples. He was crucified under Pontius Pilate at Passover, and all four Gospels testify that he rose on the third day and appeared to his followers. Everyone else in this book is here because of him.
people.quote: “Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, and the truth, and the life: no one cometh unto the Father, but by me.”

people.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
facts: Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts; also John (as “the mother of Jesus”)
paras: A young woman of Nazareth engaged to Joseph when the angel Gabriel told her she would bear the Son of the Most High (Luke 1). Her song of praise, the Magnificat, is one of the great poems of Scripture. She was at the wedding at Cana, stood at the cross, where Jesus entrusted her to the beloved disciple, and was praying with the believers in the upper room before Pentecost (Acts 1:14).
people.quote: “And Mary said, Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.”

people.name: Joseph
people.role: Carpenter of Nazareth, husband of Mary
facts: Last seen about AD 7–9, when Jesus was twelve
paras: A carpenter descended from King David. Warned in dreams, he took Mary as his wife, named the child Jesus, fled to Egypt to escape Herod the Great, and on returning avoided Herod's son Archelaus by settling in Nazareth. He is last seen when the twelve-year-old Jesus stayed behind in the temple (Luke 2). Most think he died before Jesus' public ministry, since he is never mentioned in it.
people.quote: “And Joseph arose from his sleep, and did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and took unto him his wife;”

people.name: John the Baptist
people.role: Prophet who prepared the way for Jesus
facts: Born about 6–5 BC · executed about AD 28–29
Judean wilderness, the Jordan River, Machaerus
paras: Son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, a relative of Mary. He preached repentance in the wilderness and baptized in the Jordan, then pointed his own followers to Jesus; Andrew and probably John first followed Jesus this way. He rebuked Herod Antipas for marrying his brother's wife Herodias and was beheaded in prison. The Jewish historian Josephus also records his preaching and his death at the fortress of Machaerus. Disciples of John were still found in Ephesus twenty-five years later (Acts 19:1–7).
people.quote: “On the morrow he seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold, the Lamb of God, that taketh away the sin of the world!”

people.name: Zechariah and Elizabeth
facts: The hill country of Judea; the temple in Jerusalem
paras: An elderly priest and his wife, childless for many years. While Zechariah served at the incense altar, the angel Gabriel told him they would have a

son; when he doubted he was struck mute until the boy was named John. Elizabeth's Spirit-filled greeting to the pregnant Mary (“Blessed art thou among women”) and Zechariah's song of praise, the Benedictus, frame the opening of Luke's Gospel.
people.quote: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel; For he hath visited and wrought redemption for his people,”

parts.title: The Twelve Apostles
parts.intro: Jesus chose twelve men, echoing the twelve tribes of Israel, to be with him and to be sent out. Most were ordinary working men from Galilee. Scripture says little about several of them; where only church tradition speaks, it is marked as tradition.

people.name: Simon Peter
people.role: Leader of the Twelve; preacher of Pentecost
facts: Called about AD 27 · died about AD 64–67 in Rome (tradition)
Bethsaida, Capernaum, Jerusalem, Joppa, Caesarea, Antioch, Rome
The Gospels, Acts, Galatians, 1 Corinthians, 1 and 2 Peter
paras: A fisherman from Bethsaida living in Capernaum, brought to Jesus by his brother Andrew. Jesus named him Cephas (Aramaic) or Peter (Greek), “rock.” He confessed Jesus as the Christ, denied him three times, and was restored by the Sea of Galilee. At Pentecost he preached the first gospel sermon; later his vision at Joppa and the baptism of Cornelius opened the church to Gentiles. Herod Agrippa I jailed him, and an angel freed him. Early church writers say he was crucified in Rome under Nero.
people.quote: “And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

people.name: Andrew
paras: A fisherman and first a disciple of John the Baptist. When John pointed to Jesus, Andrew followed and immediately brought his brother Simon. In John's Gospel he keeps bringing people to Jesus: the boy with five loaves and two fishes, and the Greeks who wanted to see him (John 12). Tradition says he preached around the Black Sea and in Greece and was crucified at Patrae in Achaia.
people.quote: “He findeth first his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messiah (which is, being interpreted, Christ).”

people.name: James, son of Zebedee
people.role: Apostle; one of the inner three
facts: Called about AD 27 · killed about AD 44
paras: A fisherman who left his father's boat with his brother John. Jesus named the pair Boanerges, “Sons of thunder.” With Peter and John he saw the raising of Jairus' daughter, the transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane. Herod Agrippa I had him put to death with the sword, making him the first of the Twelve to die for his faith. Often called “James the Great” to tell him apart from the other Jameses.
people.quote: “And he killed James the brother of John with the sword.”

people.name: John, son of Zebedee
people.role: Apostle; traditional author of John, 1–3 John and Revelation
facts: Called about AD 27 · died about AD 98–100 in Ephesus (tradition)
Matthew, Mark, Luke, Acts, Galatians, Revelation; traditionally the unnamed “beloved disciple” of John's Gospel and the “elder” of 2 and 3 John
paras: James' brother and one of Jesus' inner three. Church tradition identifies him with “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” who leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper and took Mary into his home. In Acts he works beside Peter, and Paul names him a “pillar” of the Jerusalem church. Early writers place his old age in Ephesus, where he led the churches of Asia, with a period of exile on Patmos under Domitian. He is the only apostle tradition says died of old age.
people.quote: “Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is begotten of God, and knoweth God.”

people.name: Philip the apostle
paras: Called by Jesus in Galilee, he at once found Nathanael and told him about Jesus. Jesus tested him before feeding the five thousand, and Greek visitors came to him asking to see Jesus. At the Last Supper he asked, “Lord, show us the Father,” drawing out Jesus' reply, “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.” Tradition says he died at Hierapolis, near Colossae. Not to be confused with Philip the evangelist (Part 4).
people.quote: “Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”

people.name: Bartholomew (Nathanael)
paras: Bartholomew appears only in the lists of the Twelve, next to Philip in all three Gospel lists. Many identify him with Nathanael of Cana, whom Philip brought to Jesus in John's Gospel. Nathanael first scoffed, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?”, but Jesus called him “an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile,” and he became one of the first to confess Jesus as Son of God. Traditions place his later preaching in India or Armenia.
people.quote: “Nathanael answered him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art King of Israel.”

people.name: Matthew (Levi)
people.role: Apostle; tax collector; traditional author of Matthew
paras: A collector of tolls and customs at Capernaum, working for Herod Antipas on the trade road by the Sea of Galilee. Tax collectors were despised as collaborators, yet Jesus called him, and Matthew threw a feast for his fellow tax collectors so they could meet Jesus. Mark and Luke call him Levi. From the second century the church has credited him with the first Gospel.
people.quote: “And as Jesus passed by from thence, he saw a man, called Matthew, sitting at the place of toll: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.”

people.name: Thomas
paras: Called Didymus, “the Twin.” He was ready to go to Judea and die with Jesus (John 11:16), honestly asked how they could know the way (John 14:5), and refused to believe the resurrection without seeing the wounds. When the risen Jesus appeared to him, he made the fullest confession in the Gospels. The Christians of southern India have long traced their church to his preaching there.
people.quote: “Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.”

people.name: James, son of Alphaeus
paras: Named in every list of the Twelve but nothing more is told of him. He may be the “James the less” whose mother Mary stood near the cross (Mark 15:40), though that is uncertain. His quiet place in Scripture is a reminder that faithful service is not always recorded.

people.name: Thaddaeus (Judas, son of James)
paras: Matthew and Mark call him Thaddaeus; Luke and Acts call him Judas the son of James. John records his one question at the Last Supper, carefully noting he was “not Iscariot.” Tradition links him with missions to Syria and Persia.
people.quote: “Judas (not Iscariot) saith unto him, Lord, what is come to pass that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?”

people.name: Simon the Zealot
paras: Called “the Cananaean” (from an Aramaic word for zeal) or “the Zealot.” The name may mean he had belonged to the movement that wanted to drive out Rome by force, or simply that he was known for zeal. Either way, Jesus placed him among the Twelve alongside Matthew, who had worked for the authorities.

people.name: Judas Iscariot
paras: The only one of the Twelve whose name may point to Judea rather than Galilee (“Iscariot” possibly means “man of Kerioth”). He kept the group's money bag and stole from it (John 12:6). He agreed with the chief priests to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver and identified him in Gethsemane with a kiss. Seized with remorse, he returned the money and died; the priests used it to buy a potter's field.
people.quote: “and said, What are ye willing to give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they weighed unto him thirty pieces of silver.”

people.name: Matthias
paras: After the ascension, Peter told the 120 believers that Judas' place must be filled by someone who had been with them from John's baptism to the ascension. Two were put forward, Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias; after prayer they cast lots and the lot fell on Matthias. Nothing more is recorded of him.
people.quote: “And they gave lots for them; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.”

parts.title: Women Who Followed and Served
parts.intro: Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his ministry, stayed at the cross and were the first witnesses of the empty tomb. In Acts and Paul's letters they host churches, teach, carry letters and raise the next generation of leaders.

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.role: Follower of Jesus; first witness of the resurrection
facts: Magdala on the Sea of Galilee; Jerusalem
paras: From Magdala, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her, and she was among the women who supported him from their own means. She watched the crucifixion and the burial, came to the tomb at dawn, and was the first to see the risen Lord and to be sent to tell the apostles. Later tradition wrongly merged her with the sinful woman of Luke 7; the Gospels do not say this.
people.quote: “Mary Magdalene cometh and telleth the disciples, I have seen the Lord; and that he had said these things unto her.”

people.name: Mary, Martha and Lazarus
paras: Two sisters and their brother whose home near Jerusalem was a place of rest for Jesus. Martha served while Mary sat at Jesus' feet (Luke 10). When Lazarus died, Jesus came four days later and raised him from the tomb, which moved the chief priests to plot against both Jesus and Lazarus. Days before the crucifixion, Mary anointed Jesus with costly ointment, and he said it was for his burial.
people.quote: “Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth on me, though he die, yet shall he live;”

people.name: Joanna and Susanna
paras: Luke names them among the women who traveled with Jesus and the Twelve and provided for them. Joanna was the wife of Chuzas, the manager of Herod Antipas' household, so the gospel had reached into the court of the ruler who killed John the Baptist. Joanna was also among the women at the empty tomb.
people.quote: “and Joanna the wife of Chuzas Herod’s steward, and Susanna, and many others, who ministered unto them of their substance.”

people.name: Mary, mother of John Mark
paras: Her large house in Jerusalem, with a gate and a servant girl named Rhoda, was where believers gathered to pray when Peter was imprisoned by Herod Agrippa I. Peter went straight there after his release. Her son John Mark, and her relative Barnabas, became missionaries.
people.quote: “And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together and were praying.”

people.name: Tabitha (Dorcas)
paras: A disciple at the port of Joppa “full of good works and almsdeeds,” who made coats and garments for the widows. When she died, the believers sent for Peter, and the widows showed him the clothes she had made. Peter prayed and she was raised to life, and many in Joppa believed. Both names mean “gazelle.”
people.quote: “Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.”

people.name: Lydia
facts: Thyatira in Asia; Philippi in Macedonia
paras: A businesswoman from Thyatira who sold costly purple cloth and worshiped God with other women at a place of prayer by the river outside Philippi. The Lord opened her heart to Paul's message; she and her household were baptized, and she insisted Paul's team stay at her home. After Paul and Silas were released from prison, they returned to her house, which became the base of the church at Philippi.
people.quote: “And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one that worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened to give heed unto the things which were spoken by Paul.”

people.name: Phoebe
people.role: Servant of the church at Cenchreae; carrier of Romans
facts: Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth; Rome
paras: Paul commends her as a servant (Greek diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae and a helper or patron of many, including himself. Because he asks the Roman believers to receive her and help her, she is almost certainly the one who carried the letter to the Romans, and she may have read and explained it to them.
people.quote: “I commend unto you Phoebe our sister, who is a servant of the church that is at Cenchreæ:”

people.name: Lois and Eunice
facts: 2 Timothy (Eunice is mentioned, unnamed, in Acts 16:1)
paras: A Jewish grandmother and mother who taught Timothy the Scriptures from childhood. Eunice was married to a Greek, and both women came to faith in Christ, probably during Paul's first journey. Paul credits their sincere faith as the root of Timothy's own.
people.quote: “having been reminded of the unfeigned faith that is in thee; which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and, I am persuaded, in thee also.”

parts.title: The Jerusalem Church and the First Spread
parts.intro: In its first years the church was centered in Jerusalem. Persecution after Stephen's death scattered believers into Judea, Samaria and beyond, and the gospel went with them, as Jesus had said in Acts 1:8.

people.name: James, the brother of Jesus
people.role: Leader of the Jerusalem church; author of James
facts: Led the church about AD 44–62 · killed AD 62
Matthew, Mark, Acts, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, James, Jude
paras: During Jesus' ministry his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5), but the risen Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7) and he became leader of the Jerusalem church. He gave the decision at the Jerusalem council that Gentiles need not be circumcised, and he received Paul's collection in AD 57. Josephus reports that the high priest Ananus had him stoned in AD 62, in the gap after the governor Festus died. Known as “James the Just.”
people.quote: “Even so faith, if it have not works, is dead in itself.”

people.name: Jude
people.role: Brother of Jesus and James; author of Jude
paras: Listed among Jesus' brothers as Judas (Mark 6:3). Like James he became a believer after the resurrection, and Paul mentions “the brethren of the Lord” traveling with their wives in ministry (1 Corinthians 9:5). His short letter calls believers to contend for the faith against false teachers and closes with one of Scripture's great doxologies.
people.quote: “Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy,”

people.name: Stephen
people.role: One of the seven; first Christian martyr
paras: A Greek-speaking Jewish believer “full of faith and of the Holy Spirit,” chosen with six others to oversee the daily food for widows. He did great wonders, and opponents brought him before the Sanhedrin, where he gave the longest speech in Acts, tracing Israel's history. He was stoned outside the city while praying for his killers. A young man named Saul watched and approved, and the persecution that followed scattered the church.
people.quote: “And they stoned Stephen, calling upon the Lord, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”

people.name: Philip the evangelist
people.role: One of the seven; first to preach in Samaria
facts: About AD 34 · still in Caesarea AD 57
Jerusalem, Samaria, the Gaza road, Caesarea
paras: Another of the seven. Scattered by persecution, he preached in Samaria with signs and many believed. Then an angel sent him to the desert road toward Gaza, where he explained Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official and baptized
him. He settled in Caesarea, and some twenty years later Paul's company stayed in his home; he had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
people.quote: “And Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this scripture, preached unto him Jesus.”

people.name: The Ethiopian official
people.role: Treasurer of the queen of Ethiopia
facts: The road from Jerusalem to Gaza; Meroë in Nubia (modern Sudan)
paras: A eunuch in charge of the treasury of Candace, the title of the queens of the Nubian kingdom of Meroë, south of Egypt. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship and was reading Isaiah aloud in his chariot when Philip joined him. Having heard the good news of Jesus, he asked to be baptized at once, and he carried the faith home to Africa.
people.quote: “And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip; and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.”

people.name: Ananias of Damascus
paras: A devout believer in Damascus whom the Lord told in a vision to go to Saul of Tarsus, the very man who had come to arrest Christians. Ananias objected, then obeyed. He laid hands on Saul, called him “Brother Saul,” and Saul's sight returned and he was baptized. Not to be confused with Ananias who lied about his gift (Acts 5) or the high priest Ananias (Part 6).
people.quote: “And Ananias departed, and entered into the house; and laying his hands on him said, Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, who appeared unto thee in the way which thou camest, hath sent me, that thou mayest receive thy sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

people.name: Agabus
paras: A prophet who came to Antioch and foretold a great famine “over all the world,” which came in the days of Claudius; the church responded by sending relief to Judea through Barnabas and Saul. Years later at Caesarea he bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem.
people.quote: “And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the Spirit that there should be a great famine over all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius.”

parts.title: Paul and His Coworkers
parts.intro: Paul rarely worked alone. His letters name dozens of men and women who traveled with him, carried his letters, led churches and suffered with him. Together they carried the gospel from Antioch to Rome.

people.name: Paul (Saul of Tarsus)
people.role: Apostle to the Gentiles; author of 13 letters
facts: Born about AD 5–10 · converted about AD 33–34 · died about AD 64–67 in Rome (tradition)
Tarsus, Jerusalem, Damascus, Antioch, Asia Minor, Greece, Ephesus, Rome
paras: A Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, born a Roman citizen, trained as a Pharisee under Gamaliel and a tentmaker by trade. He persecuted the church until the risen Jesus met him on the road to Damascus. From Antioch he made three missionary journeys (AD 46–57), planting churches across Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia and Asia, including nearly three years at Ephesus. Arrested in Jerusalem, held two years at Caesarea and taken to Rome, he wrote letters that shaped Christian teaching. Tradition says he was beheaded in Rome under Nero.
people.quote: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.”

people.name: Barnabas
people.role: Encourager; Paul's partner on the first journey
paras: A Levite from Cyprus named Joseph whom the apostles called Barnabas, which Luke translates “Son of exhortation” (or encouragement). He sold a field for the poor, vouched for the newly converted Saul when others were afraid, and was sent to lead the new mixed church at Antioch, where he brought Saul to teach. Together they made the first missionary journey. They parted over whether to take John Mark again, and Barnabas sailed with Mark to Cyprus.
people.quote: “for he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith: and much people was added unto the Lord.”

people.name: Silas (Silvanus)
people.role: Paul's partner on the second journey
facts: About AD 49–52; with Peter in the 60s
paras: A leader and prophet of the Jerusalem church, chosen to carry the council's letter to Antioch. Paul took him on the second journey; at Philippi they were beaten and jailed and sang hymns at midnight before an earthquake opened the doors. Like Paul he was a Roman citizen. He is named as co-sender of 1 and 2 Thessalonians and is named in 1 Peter 5:12 as the one through whom Peter wrote, whether as secretary or as carrier.
people.quote: “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns unto God, and the prisoners were listening to them;”

people.name: Timothy
people.role: Paul's “true child in faith”; leader at Ephesus
facts: Joined Paul about AD 49 · at Ephesus in the 60s
Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 6 of Paul's letters as co-sender, 1 and 2 Timothy, Hebrews
paras: Son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father from Lystra, well spoken of by the churches. Paul took him on the second journey and sent him on hard errands to Thessalonica, Corinth and Philippi. He is named as co-sender of 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians and Philemon. Paul left him to lead the church at Ephesus and wrote him two letters. Hebrews 13:23 says he was later released from prison.
people.quote: “Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an ensample to them that believe, in word, in manner of life, in love, in faith, in purity.”

people.name: Titus
people.role: Paul's troubleshooter in Corinth and Crete
paras: A Greek believer whom Paul took to Jerusalem as a test case; the leaders did not require him to be circumcised. Paul sent him to Corinth during the church's hardest season, and his report brought Paul great comfort (2 Corinthians 7). He organized the collection for Jerusalem, was left in Crete to appoint elders, and was last heard of in Dalmatia on the Adriatic coast.
people.quote: “For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that were wanting, and appoint elders in every city, as I gave thee charge;”

people.name: Luke
people.role: Physician; author of Luke and Acts
facts: Colossians, Philemon, 2 Timothy (and the “we” passages of Acts)
paras: Paul calls him “the beloved physician.” He was probably a Gentile, since Paul lists him apart from his Jewish coworkers (Colossians 4:10–14). Where Acts switches to “we,” the author was traveling with Paul, including the shipwreck voyage to Rome. His two volumes make up over a quarter of the New Testament, and he stayed with Paul to the end.
people.quote: “Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee; for he is useful to me for ministering.”

people.name: John Mark
paras: Son of Mary of Jerusalem and cousin of Barnabas. He went with Barnabas and Saul on the first journey but turned back at Perga, which later split the two leaders. He was restored: Paul names him as a fellow worker in Rome and later asks for him as “useful to me for ministering.” Peter calls him “Mark my son,” and early writers say his Gospel preserves Peter's preaching.
people.quote: “She that is in Babylon, elect together with you, saluteth you; and so doth Mark my son.”

people.name: Priscilla and Aquila
paras: A Jewish couple from Rome, Aquila a native of Pontus, who came to Corinth when Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome about AD 49. Paul lived and worked with them as a tentmaker. They moved with him to Ephesus, explained the way of God more accurately to Apollos, and hosted a church in their home there. Paul later greets them back in Rome and says they had risked their necks for him. Paul usually names Priscilla (Prisca) first.
people.quote: “Salute Prisca and Aquila my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus,”

people.name: Apollos
paras: A Jew of Alexandria, eloquent and “mighty in the scriptures,” who taught accurately about Jesus but knew only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila took him aside in Ephesus and explained more fully. He went on to Corinth and powerfully refuted opponents, and some Corinthians began saying “I am of Apollos.” Paul treated him as a valued partner, not a rival. Some have suggested he wrote Hebrews.
people.quote: “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.”

people.name: Tychicus
paras: A believer from Asia, one of the delegates who traveled with Paul as he took the collection toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). During Paul's Roman imprisonment he carried the letters to the Ephesians and Colossians, with Onesimus beside him, and was to report on Paul's situation in person. Paul later sent him to Ephesus again and considered sending him to Crete.
people.quote: “But that ye also may know my affairs, how I do, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, shall make known to you all things:”

people.name: Epaphras
people.role: Founder of the church at Colossae
paras: A Colossian who heard the gospel, probably during Paul's years at Ephesus, and took it home to the Lycus valley, planting the church at Colossae and working for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis. He came to Paul in Rome with news of the church and its troubles, which led to the letter to the Colossians. Paul calls him a fellow prisoner who was always “striving” for the churches in prayer.
people.quote: “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, saluteth you, always striving for you in his prayers, that ye may stand perfect and fully assured in all the will of God.”

people.name: Epaphroditus
paras: Sent by the church at Philippi to bring Paul a gift in prison and to serve him. He fell so ill that he nearly died, and was distressed that the Philippians had heard. Paul sent him home, probably carrying the letter to the Philippians, with instructions to honor him as a brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier.
people.quote: “But I counted it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow-worker and fellow-soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need;”

people.name: Aristarchus
paras: A believer from Thessalonica who was seized by the mob in the riot at Ephesus and dragged into the theater. He went with Paul to Jerusalem and sailed with him on the voyage to Rome, through the shipwreck. Paul calls him “my fellow-prisoner.”
people.quote: “Aristarchus my fellow-prisoner saluteth you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (touching whom ye received commandments; if he come unto you, receive him),”

people.name: Philemon and Onesimus
people.role: A master and his runaway slave, made brothers
paras: Philemon was a believer at Colossae whose home hosted the church. His slave Onesimus ran away, met Paul in Rome and came to faith. Paul sent him back with Tychicus and a personal letter asking Philemon to receive him “no longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved.” Around AD 110 a bishop of Ephesus was named Onesimus; some think it was the same man.
people.quote: “no longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much rather to thee, both in the flesh and in the Lord.”

people.name: Erastus
people.role: City treasurer of Corinth; Paul's helper
paras: Paul sent him with Timothy from Ephesus to Macedonia, and from Corinth Paul sent greetings from “Erastus the treasurer of the city.” A paving stone
still in place at Corinth records that an Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense as aedile, a city official. Many think it is the same man, a Roman official who served the gospel.
people.quote: “Gaius my host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the treasurer of the city saluteth you, and Quartus the brother.”

people.name: Demas
paras: Named alongside Luke as Paul's fellow worker during the first Roman imprisonment. In Paul's last letter, however, Demas has gone to Thessalonica, having “loved this present world.” His story is a sober warning set beside the faithfulness of others in this book.
people.quote: “for Demas forsook me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.”

parts.title: Jewish Leaders
parts.intro: Judea was governed day to day by the high priest and the Sanhedrin, the ruling council of about seventy elders, priests and scribes, under Roman oversight. From AD 6 Rome appointed and removed the high priests, and from AD 41 the Herodian kings Rome put in charge did so. Some leaders opposed Jesus; others quietly followed him.

people.name: Annas
people.role: Former high priest; head of a priestly dynasty
paras: Appointed high priest by the Roman governor Quirinius and removed by Valerius Gratus, he remained the power behind the office. Five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held it after him. Jesus was taken to Annas first
after his arrest, and Annas sat with the council that questioned Peter and John (Acts 4:6).
people.quote: “and led him to Annas first; for he was father in law to Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.”

people.name: Caiaphas
paras: Joseph Caiaphas held office for eighteen years, longer than any high priest in the Roman period, which suggests he worked well with Pilate. He argued that it was better for one man to die than for the nation to perish, and he presided at Jesus' night hearing. He was removed in AD 36, about when Pilate was. In 1990 a family bone box inscribed “Joseph son of Caiaphas” was found in Jerusalem.
people.quote: “nor do ye take account that it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.”

people.name: Gamaliel
paras: A Pharisee and teacher of the law honored by all the people, remembered in Jewish tradition as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. When the council wanted to kill the apostles, he urged caution: if this movement is from men it will fail, but if it is from God they cannot stop it. Paul says he was brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel.”
people.quote: “but if it is of God, ye will not be able to overthrow them; lest haply ye be found even to be fighting against God.”

people.name: Nicodemus
people.role: Pharisee and member of the council
paras: A Pharisee and “ruler of the Jews” who came to Jesus by night and heard that a man must be born anew. Later he reminded the council that the law does not condemn a man without a hearing. After the crucifixion he openly brought about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes and helped Joseph of Arimathea bury Jesus.
people.quote: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth on him should not perish, but have eternal life.”

people.name: Joseph of Arimathea
paras: A rich and respected member of the council who had not agreed with its decision against Jesus and was secretly his disciple. On the evening of the crucifixion he boldly asked Pilate for the body and laid it in his own new tomb cut in the rock, which Christians have long seen as fulfilling Isaiah 53:9.
people.quote: “there came Joseph of Arimathæa, a councillor of honorable estate, who also himself was looking for the kingdom of God; and he boldly went in unto Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.”

people.name: Ananias, son of Nedebaeus
facts: High priest about AD 47–59 · killed AD 66
paras: Appointed by Herod of Chalcis and known from Josephus as greedy and violent. When Paul spoke before the council he ordered him struck on the mouth, and Paul called him a “whited wall.” He traveled to Caesarea to
accuse Paul before Felix. At the start of the Jewish revolt in AD 66, rebels killed him.
people.quote: “And the high priest Ananias commanded them that stood by him to smite him on the mouth.”

parts.title: The Herod Family
parts.intro: The Herods were an Idumean family whom Rome made kings and princes over the Jews. Several different men in the New Testament are simply called “Herod,” so the dates and territories here help tell them apart.

people.name: Herod the Great
paras: Named “king of the Jews” by the Roman Senate in 40 BC, he won his kingdom by 37 BC. A brilliant builder, he rebuilt the Jerusalem temple on a vast scale and built the port of Caesarea and the fortresses of Masada and Herodium. He was also ruthless, killing a wife and three sons. Jesus was born near the end of his reign; when the wise men came seeking the newborn king, Herod ordered the boys of Bethlehem killed. He died in 4 BC, and his kingdom was divided among three sons.
people.quote: “Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judæa in the days of Herod the king, behold, Wise-men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying,”

people.name: Archelaus
paras: Herod's son who received Judea, Samaria and Idumea with the lesser title of ethnarch. He began his rule by massacring about 3,000 people at a Passover. Joseph, returning from Egypt, feared him and settled in Galilee instead. After complaints from both Jews and Samaritans, Augustus banished him to
Gaul in AD 6, and Judea came under direct Roman governors. Jesus' parable of a nobleman who went to a far country to receive a kingdom (Luke 19:12) may echo his story.
people.quote: “But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judæa in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither; and being warned of God in a dream, he withdrew into the parts of Galilee,”

people.name: Herod Antipas
facts: Tiberias and Sepphoris in Galilee; Machaerus in Perea
paras: The Herod of Jesus' ministry, ruling as tetrarch over Galilee and Perea. He built Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee and named it for the emperor. He married Herodias, his half-brother's wife, imprisoned John the Baptist for condemning it, and beheaded him at a birthday feast. Jesus called him “that fox.” Pilate sent Jesus to him during the trial, and he mocked him. Caligula exiled him to Gaul in AD 39.
people.quote: “And he said unto them, Go and say to that fox, Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures to-day and to-morrow, and the third day I am perfected.”

people.name: Herodias and her daughter
paras: A granddaughter of Herod the Great who left her husband, a half-brother of Antipas, to marry Antipas. She held a grudge against John the Baptist for condemning the marriage. When her daughter danced for Antipas and was promised anything she asked, Herodias told her to ask for John's head. Josephus names the daughter Salome. Herodias chose to follow Antipas into exile.
people.quote: “And she went out, and said unto her mother, What shall I ask? And she said, The head of John the Baptizer.”

people.name: Philip the tetrarch
paras: Herod's son who received the lands northeast of the Sea of Galilee, Iturea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1). He was regarded as the mildest of the brothers. He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea Philippi, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ, and enlarged Bethsaida, the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip. He married Salome, Herodias' daughter.

people.name: Herod Agrippa I
paras: A grandson of Herod the Great raised in Rome and friend of the future emperors Caligula and Claudius. Caligula gave him Philip's territory and then Antipas'; Claudius added Judea, briefly restoring his grandfather's kingdom. To please the Jewish leaders he killed James son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter. At Caesarea in AD 44 the crowd hailed him as a god; Acts says an angel struck him and he died, and Josephus tells a closely matching story.
people.quote: “And immediately an angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.”

people.name: Herod Agrippa II and Bernice
paras: Son of Agrippa I, he ruled territories in the north and had the right to appoint Jerusalem's high priests. In AD 59 he and his sister Bernice visited the new governor Festus, who asked them to hear Paul. Paul's defense moved him to reply that Paul was trying to make him a Christian. He sided
with Rome in the Jewish revolt. Bernice later had a long affair with the future emperor Titus. Another sister, Drusilla, married the governor Felix.
people.quote: “And Agrippa said unto Paul, With but little persuasion thou wouldest fain make me a Christian.”

parts.title: The Roman Emperors
parts.intro: The New Testament usually calls the emperor simply “Caesar.” This part covers eight emperors, from Augustus to Domitian, under whom the New Testament story unfolded. Only three are named in the text, but all of them shaped the world the gospel traveled through.

people.name: Augustus
paras: Born Octavian, the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar. After defeating Antony and Cleopatra he ended a century of civil war and took the title Augustus, “revered one.” His long peace, the Pax Romana, with safe roads and sea lanes, later made travel easy for missionaries. Inscriptions hailed him as “son of a god” and his birthday as “good news” for the world. Luke sets Jesus' birth beside his decree for a census.
people.quote: “Now it came to pass in those days, there went out a decree from Cæsar Augustus, that all the world should be enrolled.”

people.name: Tiberius
paras: Augustus' stepson and successor, a capable general but a suspicious, withdrawn ruler who spent his last years on Capri. Luke dates John the Baptist's preaching to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, about AD 28–29. The silver denarius shown to Jesus probably bore his image, and the city of
Tiberias was named for him. Jesus was crucified, and the church was born, during his reign.
people.quote: “And Jesus said unto them, Render unto Cæsar the things that are Cæsar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s. And they marvelled greatly at him.”

people.name: Caligula (Gaius)
facts: Not named in the New Testament
paras: Tiberius' great-nephew, who began popular and became cruel and erratic, demanding worship as a living god. In AD 40 he ordered his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple, which would have sparked war; the governor of Syria delayed, Agrippa I pleaded, and Caligula was murdered before it happened. Many readers hear echoes of this crisis in the warnings of Mark 13:14 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4.

people.name: Claudius
people.role: Emperor who expelled the Jews from Rome
paras: Made emperor by the guard after Caligula's murder. Acts names him twice: a great famine came in his reign, and he ordered all Jews to leave Rome, which brought Priscilla and Aquila to Corinth. The Roman writer Suetonius says the Jews were expelled for disturbances “at the instigation of Chrestus,” probably arguments over Christ. An inscription from his reign at Delphi dates Gallio's term in Corinth and anchors the timeline of Paul's life.
people.quote: “And he found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome: and he came unto them;”

people.name: Nero
people.role: Emperor of Paul's appeal and the first persecution
paras: Emperor at sixteen. His early reign was stable, and it was to Nero that Paul appealed as a Roman citizen. Believers were even found in Caesar's household. After the great fire of Rome in AD 64, Nero blamed the Christians and had many put to death, some burned as torches, according to Tacitus. Peter and Paul are traditionally said to have died in this period. He took his own life in AD 68.
people.quote: “All the saints salute you, especially they that are of Cæsar’s household.”

people.name: Vespasian
people.role: General of the Jewish war; emperor
facts: Not named in the New Testament
paras: Nero sent him to crush the Jewish revolt in AD 67, and he conquered Galilee. After Nero's death, AD 69 became the “year of the four emperors” (Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian); Vespasian won and left the siege of Jerusalem to his son Titus. He began the Colosseum, partly paid for with treasure taken from the temple.

people.name: Titus
facts: Not named in the New Testament
paras: Vespasian's son, who besieged Jerusalem in AD 70. The temple burned and the city was destroyed, about forty years after Jesus wept over it and warned that not one stone would be left on another. The Arch of Titus in Rome still shows soldiers carrying the temple's lampstand. Not the same person as Paul's coworker Titus.
people.quote: “But when ye see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that her desolation is at hand.”

people.name: Domitian
people.role: Emperor in the time of Revelation
facts: Not named in the New Testament
paras: Titus' younger brother, an autocrat who liked to be addressed as “our lord and god.” The emperor cult flourished in Asia, and Ephesus built a large temple to his family. Early church writers date John's exile to Patmos and the writing of Revelation to his reign, and Revelation's call to worship God alone, not the beast, spoke directly to churches under that pressure. How widely he persecuted Christians is debated.
people.quote: “I John, your brother and partaker with you in the tribulation and kingdom and patience which are in Jesus, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.”

parts.title: Roman Governors, Soldiers and Officials
parts.intro: Roman officials appear at nearly every turn of the story: governors who judged, soldiers who guarded, and city officers who kept order. Luke records many of them accurately by their correct local titles, and several are confirmed by inscriptions.

people.name: Quirinius
paras: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius was a senior Roman statesman. As governor of Syria he carried out the census of Judea in AD 6, when Archelaus was removed, and that census sparked the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). Luke links the census at Jesus' birth with Quirinius; because Herod
died in 4 BC, scholars debate whether this refers to an earlier role of Quirinius or should be read as the census “before” his.
people.quote: “This was the first enrolment made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.”

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.role: Governor of Judea who sentenced Jesus
facts: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, 1 Timothy
paras: The Roman prefect of Judea, based at Caesarea and in Jerusalem for the feasts. Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and provocative, and Luke 13:1 mentions Galileans he killed. He found no crime in Jesus but gave in to the crowd and the threat of being called no friend of Caesar. In 1961 a stone naming “Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea” was found at Caesarea. He was recalled to Rome in AD 36.
people.quote: “Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find no crime in him.”

people.name: The centurions of the Gospels
paras: A centurion commanded about eighty men. At Capernaum a centurion who had built the synagogue asked Jesus to heal his servant with just a word, and Jesus said he had not found such faith in Israel. At the cross, the centurion in charge watched how Jesus died and declared him the Son of God.
people.quote: “And when the centurion, who stood by over against him, saw that he so gave up the ghost, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God.”

people.name: Cornelius
paras: A centurion of the Italian cohort at Caesarea, a God-fearer who prayed and gave generously. An angel told him to send for Peter, while at Joppa Peter saw a vision of clean and unclean animals. As Peter preached in his house, the Holy Spirit fell on the Gentile listeners, and they were baptized. This moment, defended by Peter in Jerusalem, opened the church to the nations.
people.quote: “And Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:”

people.name: Sergius Paulus
paras: The governor of Cyprus when Barnabas and Saul arrived on their first journey. An intelligent man, he called for them to hear the word of God, while his court magician Elymas opposed them and was struck blind. Seeing this, the proconsul believed. From this point Acts calls Saul by his Roman name, Paul. Inscriptions name members of the Sergius Paulus family near Pisidian Antioch, the next place Paul went.
people.quote: “Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord.”

people.name: Gallio
paras: Lucius Junius Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca. When the Jews of Corinth brought Paul before his judgment seat, he refused to hear the case, treating it as a dispute about Jewish law. His ruling gave the church in Corinth room to grow. An inscription found at Delphi fixes his term and so
helps date Paul's eighteen months in Corinth. He is said to have died, perhaps by his own hand, in Nero's purges about AD 65.
people.quote: “but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves; I am not minded to be a judge of these matters.”

people.name: The town clerk and the Asiarchs of Ephesus
paras: During the riot over Artemis, some of the Asiarchs, leading men of the province who oversaw the imperial cult, were friendly to Paul and urged him not to enter the theater. The town clerk, the chief civic officer, finally quieted the crowd, pointing out that the Christians had robbed no temple and that the courts were open. He warned that Rome might charge the city with rioting.
people.quote: “And when the townclerk had quieted the multitude, he saith, Ye men of Ephesus, what man is there who knoweth not that the city of the Ephesians is temple-keeper of the great Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter?”

people.name: Claudius Lysias
paras: The tribune in charge of about a thousand soldiers at the fortress beside the temple. He rescued Paul from a mob and nearly had him flogged before learning he was a Roman citizen; Lysias had bought his own citizenship at great cost. When a plot to kill Paul was uncovered, he sent him to Caesarea by night under heavy guard with a letter to Felix.
people.quote: “And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this citizenship. And Paul said, But I am a Roman born.”

people.name: Felix
paras: Antonius Felix, a former slave who rose through his brother Pallas' influence at court. Tacitus said he wielded a king's power with the mind of a slave. He married Drusilla, a daughter of Agrippa I. He heard Paul's defense and later listened to him speak of righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, and was afraid; but he kept Paul in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.
people.quote: “And as he reasoned of righteousness, and self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answered, Go thy way for this time; and when I have a convenient season, I will call thee unto me.”

people.name: Festus
people.role: Governor who sent Paul to Caesar
paras: Porcius Festus succeeded Felix and wanted to settle Paul's case quickly. When he proposed a trial in Jerusalem, Paul used his right as a citizen and appealed to Caesar. Unsure what charge to send, Festus consulted Agrippa II. He died in office about AD 62, and in the gap before the next governor arrived, James the Lord's brother was killed.
people.quote: “Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, Thou hast appealed unto Cæsar: unto Cæsar shalt thou go.”

people.name: Julius the centurion
people.role: Officer who escorted Paul to Rome
paras: A centurion of the Augustan cohort placed in charge of Paul and other prisoners for the voyage to Rome. He treated Paul kindly, letting him visit
friends at Sidon. When the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners during the shipwreck, Julius stopped them in order to save Paul.
people.quote: “And the next day we touched at Sidon: and Julius treated Paul kindly, and gave him leave to go unto his friends and refresh himself.”

people.name: Publius
paras: The leading official of Malta, where the shipwrecked party landed. He welcomed them for three days, and Paul healed his father of fever and dysentery. Others on the island then came to be healed, and the islanders honored the travelers and supplied them when they sailed. The same Greek title, “first man” of the island, appears on inscriptions found on Malta.
people.quote: “Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius; who received us, and entertained us three days courteously.”

parts.title: Opponents and Others Along the Way
parts.intro: Not everyone welcomed the gospel. These people opposed the apostles, profited from idolatry or caused trouble inside the churches.

people.name: Simon the sorcerer
paras: A magician who had amazed Samaria and been called “that power of God which is called Great.” He believed and was baptized under Philip, but when he saw the Spirit given through the apostles' hands he offered money to buy that power. Peter sternly rebuked him. Buying church office came to be called “simony” after him.
people.quote: “But Peter said unto him, Thy silver perish with thee, because thou hast thought to obtain the gift of God with money.”

people.name: Elymas (Bar-Jesus)
paras: A Jewish false prophet attached to the proconsul Sergius Paulus. When he tried to turn the governor from the faith, Paul declared him blind for a time, and mist and darkness fell on him. His defeat led to the proconsul's belief.
people.quote: “And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season. And immediately there fell on him a mist and a darkness; and he went about seeking some to lead him by the hand.”

people.name: Demetrius the silversmith
people.role: Leader of the riot at Ephesus
paras: He made silver shrines of Artemis and saw that Paul's preaching, that gods made with hands are no gods, was hurting the trade across Asia. He stirred the craftsmen, the city filled with confusion, and a crowd shouted for two hours in the great theater. The riot shows how far the gospel had reached into the economy and religion of Ephesus.
people.quote: “And when they heard this they were filled with wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.”

people.name: Alexander the coppersmith
paras: Paul warns Timothy, then leading the church in Ephesus, that Alexander the coppersmith did him much harm and strongly opposed his message. He may be the same Alexander Paul had handed over to Satan with Hymenaeus for making shipwreck of the faith (1 Timothy 1:20).
people.quote: “Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord will render to him according to his works:”

people.name: Diotrephes
people.role: Church leader who loved to be first
facts: A church in the province of Asia
paras: A leader who refused to accept John's letter or his authority, spread false charges against him, would not welcome traveling missionaries and expelled those who did. John contrasts him with Demetrius, who had a good report from everyone. He is a picture of how love of position can harm a church.
people.quote: “I wrote somewhat unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.”
